lead: Power and efficiency come from four levers: more trapped air, better air-fuel mixing, less friction, and better control. Engine makers rarely find one large gain; they stack small gains. A turbocharger, a high-pressure injector, low-friction oil and a closed-loop ECU each move brake power, brake specific fuel consumption (BSFC) or both. Road cars, trucks and gensets use these levers, then prove the result on a standard test. Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic.
prereq: You need: the variables in the chapter on variables affecting performance; the turbocharger hardware is covered under Supercharging: objectives, types and effects.

blocks.text: Each lever changes a measurable variable. More air raises trapped mass. Better mixing shortens and shapes the burn. Less friction raises brake power for the same indicated power. Better control keeps the engine near its best point.

items: More air: turbocharging or supercharging raises intake density; an intercooler lowers charge temperature and raises density again. Four valves and good ports cut pumping loss; variable valve timing (VVT) moves the torque band.

Better mixture: high-pressure common rail direct injection (CRDI) gives a finer spray; electronic injection timing places the burn near top dead centre (TDC); chamber shape adds swirl, squish or tumble.
Less friction: low-viscosity oil with friction modifiers, surface coatings, lighter reciprocating parts, and better rings and bearings cut friction mean effective pressure (FMEP).
Better control: a closed-loop engine control unit (ECU) uses a lambda sensor to hold air-fuel ratio and a knock sensor to protect spark advance.

blocks.text: The levers interact: more air needs more fuel, and control keeps the extra air useful.

Changing the cycle can raise efficiency more than any single part. Miller or Atkinson operation closes the intake valve early or late, so the expansion stroke is longer than the effective compression stroke. The engine extracts more work from the same fuel. A higher compression ratio does the same, but it is limited by knock in spark-ignition (SI) engines and by peak pressure in compression-ignition (CI) engines. In a turbocharged engine, Miller timing also lowers knock and turbine inlet temperature, so boost can rise. Cylinder deactivation and stop-start are control changes: they cut pumping and idle losses when demand is low.

blocks.where: η<sub>Otto</sub> is the ideal Otto cycle efficiency; r is the compression ratio; γ is the ratio of specific heats, 1.4 for air. With Miller or Atkinson timing the effective compression ratio, set by intake valve closing, is lower than the geometric one, while the expansion ratio stays geometric; that difference is where the gain comes from, so do not put the geometric ratio straight into this formula.

blocks.text: The ideal gain is set by the compression ratio. These changes must keep combustion stable; too much Miller timing hurts combustion and torque. In practice, the valve event is tuned with the boost level.

Every step that raises power or efficiency usually raises oxides of nitrogen (NOx) or cost. More air raises peak pressure and temperature; advancing the injection timing raises NOx; thinner oil cuts friction but can let metal touch and wear at high load; aggressive Miller timing can hurt combustion. A boost increase must be matched by fuel, or the mixture leans and power falls; the knock limit or turbine inlet temperature sets the ceiling, not the boost number. A change that wins on one point may lose on another. The engine must be proved on a standard test, not a single best point. A performance claim is brake power, BSFC and emissions at defined speed-load points. Test procedure and in-cylinder pressure are in the chapter on testing standards and pressure measurement.

Use a dynamometer and repeat the same test conditions before and after. The trade-off is why a production engine is a compromise: driveability, fuel quality, durability and emission limits all pull against the peak number.

spec.aria: Four rows: more air raises trapped mass, better mixture speeds the burn, less friction cuts friction power, better control holds the best point.

examples.question: A 2.0 L naturally aspirated petrol engine gives 80 kW. A turbocharger with an intercooler raises intake air density to 1.4 times ambient. Assume the same volumetric efficiency and air-fuel ratio. The BSFC is 240 g/kWh. Find the new power and the new fuel flow.
steps: Air density ratio = 1.4. At the same air-fuel ratio, power scales with trapped air mass: P<sub>new</sub> = P<sub>old</sub> × 1.4.
Fuel flow = BSFC × brake power. New: 240 g/kWh × 112 kW = 26,880 g/h = 26.88 kg/h.
examples.answer: The new power is 112 kW, a 40 % gain, and the new fuel flow is 26.88 kg/h against 19.2 kg/h before.
examples.check:
p<sub>old</sub> = 80.0
ratio = 1.4
p<sub>new</sub> = p<sub>old</sub> * ratio
gain = (p<sub>new</sub> - p<sub>old</sub>) / p<sub>old</sub> * 100.0
bsfc = 240.0
flow<sub>new</sub> = bsfc * p<sub>new</sub> / 1000.0
flow<sub>old</sub> = bsfc * p<sub>old</sub> / 1000.0
print(p<sub>new</sub>)
print(gain)
print(flow<sub>new</sub>)
print(flow<sub>old</sub>)

examples.question: A petrol engine of compression ratio 9.5 gives 60 kW brake power with an indicated power of 72 kW. A new head raises the compression ratio to 11, and low-friction oil cuts the friction power by 15 %. Take γ = 1.4 and assume the indicated thermal efficiency rises in the same ratio as the Otto efficiency, at the same fuel flow. Find the new brake power.
steps: Ratio: 0.6168 ÷ 0.5936 = 1.0390, so the new indicated power is 72 × 1.0390 = 74.81 kW.
Old friction power: 72 − 60 = 12 kW. New: 12 × 0.85 = 10.2 kW.
New brake power: 74.81 − 10.2 = 64.61 kW, a gain of 4.61 kW (7.7 %) for the same fuel.
examples.answer: About 64.6 kW, up from 60 kW: 2.81 kW from the higher compression ratio and 1.8 kW from the lower friction.

traps: Boost alone does not raise power: fuel must rise by the same ratio, and the knock limit or turbine inlet temperature sets the ceiling.
Miller or Atkinson timing is not just a longer expansion stroke; valve timing must keep combustion stable.
Low-viscosity oil is not always better; it must protect the bearing film at high load.
A higher compression ratio raises ideal efficiency but can cause knock or exceed peak-pressure limits.

quiz.q: Name the four families of performance improvements.
quiz.a: More air, better mixture, less friction and better control.

quiz.q: Why does an intercooler help a turbocharged engine?
quiz.a: It lowers intake temperature, raises air density and reduces knock, so more air and fuel can be burned.

quiz.q: A 60 kW engine gets 1.25 times air density at the same air-fuel ratio. Find the new power.
A tuner raises boost but keeps fuel flow fixed. Predict power and emissions.
quiz.a: With the fuel fixed, the extra air only leans the mixture. Power stays roughly where it was, because the fuel sets the energy input, or falls if a petrol engine becomes too lean and misfires; exhaust temperature and NOx can rise near φ ≈ 0.9. Fuel must rise with the air to gain power.
Valve opening and closing timing, so trapped air and the torque band change.

quiz.q: Why can cylinder deactivation save fuel?
quiz.a: It cuts pumping and idle losses at low load by working fewer cylinders.

quiz.q: BSFC is 250 g/kWh at 90 kW. Find fuel flow in kg/h.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production engines now combine Miller timing, high compression, 48 V electric boost and model-based ECU control. Formula Student and motorsport teams log in-cylinder pressure and use it to tune boost and injection. Search for right-sizing, variable compression ratio and low-temperature combustion to see where these levers meet emissions. The next step is calibration on a transient dynamometer, not a steady-state point.
